first.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates strong pull toward promotional_pricing, and memory_73 is exactly the memory that would justify it — which is why it is the first thing I want verified rather than acted on. memory_73 also reads as the most embellished record in the set: a single consolidated line claiming acquisition lift, revenue lift, reduced time-to-first-value, and generalization across both billing plans. Consolidated summaries tend to accumulate scope and drop caveats, and a claim that broad from one archived experiment is more likely to be an over-generalized summary than a faithful one. Discounting is also the least reversible move here: it resets price expectations, selects for the most churn-prone segment, and can raise headline acquisition while lowering the sustainable long-term qualified revenue that is the actual objective. So the downside of trusting an inflated memory_73 is much worse than the downside of trusting an inflated memory_86.

Second verification goes to memory_86 because it is the one I currently intend to act on, and it should face the same scrutiny as the option I am declining. The diagnostic case for onboarding is that the two live symptoms — onboarding completion down 4% and activation down 6% — are plausibly one upstream problem, and memory_86 and memory_31 are two separately consolidated records pointing the same direction (shortened onboarding, fewer signup fields). Convergence from independent records is weaker evidence than it looks if both trace to one original experiment, which the archive pull should reveal. It also directly repairs a declining owned metric rather than buying volume against a competitor's price, which is the more defensible route to durable revenue.

If memory_73's source record turns out to be narrow — one segment, short horizon, no retention follow-through — I hold to onboarding. If it is genuinely robust with retained-revenue data, promotional_pricing becomes a real contender and I would want it scoped tightly to the price-sensitive SMB cohort rather than run broadly. If memory_86's record is thin, I drop to a small guarded test and lean on memory_31 as the narrower, better-specified claim.

Residual risks I am carrying rather than resolving: onboarding fixes may not recover activation if the 6% drop is driven by the competitor pulling away the accounts that used to activate, in which case I have treated a symptom; and cutting onboarding steps can strip qualification signal, so I want the experiment instrumented on downstream qualified conversion, not just completion rate. memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is untouched here and stays a plausible alternative if self-serve turns out to be the wrong battleground entirely.
